eras.name: Early computers
eras.background: The first modern computers kept their programs in memory alongside data. IBM then defined one instruction set for a whole family of machines. Its fastest models introduced caches and out-of-order execution.

eras.name: Microprocessors
eras.background: Integrated circuits put a whole processor on one chip, and Moore's law kept doubling the transistors on it. Simple RISC instruction sets let those chips pipeline well. Growing transistor budgets went into caches, branch prediction and out-of-order execution.

eras.name: Multicore
eras.background: Faster clocks and deeper speculation made chips too hot and wasted energy on discarded work. Vendors put several cores on each chip instead, and GPUs opened their many simple cores to general programs. Finding the parallelism became the job of software.

eras.name: Specialization
eras.background: With Moore's law slowing and Dennard scaling over, general-purpose chips gained only a few percent a year. Architects turned to chips built for one domain and to open instruction sets. RowHammer and Spectre exposed the security cost of density and speculation.

nodes.label: Stored program
nodes.problem: ENIAC's programs were set up by hand on plugboards and switches.
nodes.idea: Keep instructions in read-write memory beside the data, as Manchester's Baby first did.
nodes.impact: Most early computers drew on von Neumann's EDVAC report, and the idea still defines a modern computer.

nodes.label: System/360
nodes.idea: IBM runs one instruction set across a family of models, cheap to fast, using microcode.
nodes.impact: It defined architecture as what programmers see, separate from how each model is built.

from.why: Each machine line had its own instruction set, and IBM alone had four incompatible lines.

nodes.label: Tomasulo
nodes.problem: Fast arithmetic units sat idle while instructions waited on results from earlier ones.
nodes.idea: IBM's Model 91 tags pending results, so each instruction starts as soon as its operands arrive.
nodes.impact: Its tagging scheme later made out-of-order processors possible.

nodes.label: Cache
nodes.problem: Main memory large enough for programs was far slower than the processor.
nodes.idea: IBM's Model 85 keeps recently used memory in a small, fast cache that programs cannot see.
nodes.impact: Programs ran unchanged but faster, and CPUs today use several levels of cache.

nodes.label: RISC
nodes.idea: Patterson and Ditzel propose a few simple instructions one chip can run fast, with compilers doing the rest.
nodes.impact: Berkeley's RISC-I and Stanford's MIPS proved it, and nearly all processors today are RISC.

from.why: Microcoded instruction sets kept growing, yet compilers used only a few simple instructions.

nodes.label: MESI
nodes.idea: Papamarcos and Patel mark each cached block exclusive or shared and invalidate other copies only when shared.
nodes.impact: Its four states were later named MESI, and almost all commercial protocols keep its exclusive state.

from.why: With a private cache per processor, one could change its copy while others kept stale ones.

nodes.label: Pentium Pro
nodes.idea: Intel's Pentium Pro decodes x86 into micro-ops and runs them out of order, speculating past branches.
nodes.impact: Intel and AMD closed the gap with RISC, and most fast processors still work this way.

from.why: Supplied out-of-order scheduling, which growing transistor budgets could now fit on one chip.
Simple RISC instructions pipelined well, while complex x86 instructions did not.

nodes.label: Multicore
nodes.idea: Intel and AMD ship dual-core processors, adding cores instead of raising clock rates.
nodes.impact: Software now had to find the parallelism, and Amdahl's law capped the gains.

from.why: Higher clock rates and deeper speculation pushed power and heat past what chips could shed.

nodes.label: CUDA
nodes.idea: NVIDIA's CUDA runs C programs as many threads, grouped into blocks that share memory.
nodes.impact: GPUs became general parallel processors, and AlexNet was trained on them with CUDA code.

from.why: Chips were now parallel and GPUs had the most cores, but they were programmed through awkward graphics APIs.

nodes.label: RISC-V
nodes.idea: Berkeley researchers design an open, royalty-free instruction set with a small base and optional extensions.
nodes.impact: A nonprofit foundation now runs it, and anyone can build RISC-V cores without fees.

from.why: Successful RISC sets such as ARM required licenses that shut out academia and small companies.

nodes.label: RowHammer
nodes.problem: DRAM cells packed ever closer began to leak charge into their neighbors.
nodes.idea: CMU and Intel researchers show that activating one row repeatedly flips bits in nearby rows of most modules.
nodes.impact: Google's Project Zero turned it into a kernel exploit, so memory reliability became a security issue.

nodes.label: TPU
nodes.idea: Google's TPU trades caches and speculation for a large matrix unit and software-managed memory.
nodes.impact: It served Google search, translation and AlphaGo, and made the case for domain-specific chips.

from.why: CPUs and GPUs spent hardware on average throughput, while serving neural networks needs fast, predictable responses.

nodes.label: Spectre
nodes.idea: Mistrain the branch predictor so a victim speculatively reads secrets, then recover them through cache timing.
nodes.impact: Most fast CPUs were affected, and kernels, compilers and chips added defenses that cost speed.

from.why: Speculative work was assumed invisible once discarded, yet it left traces in the caches.

main.title: UC Berkeley CS 61C: Great Ideas in Computer Architecture
main.why: C and number representation, RISC-V assembly, the datapath and five-stage pipeline, caches, SIMD and thread-level parallelism, and virtual memory. In English.

main.title: A New Golden Age for Computer Architecture
main.why: How instruction sets went from microcode to RISC, why general-purpose speedups stalled, and why domain-specific chips and open ISAs come next.

further.title: The Case for the Reduced Instruction Set Computer

main.title: An Efficient Algorithm for Exploiting Multiple Arithmetic Units
main.why: Execution units idled behind instructions waiting on results, so Tomasulo's algorithm renames registers with tags and starts each instruction when its operands arrive.

main.title: A case for (partially) TAgged GEometric history length branch prediction
main.why: Each wrong branch guess flushes a deep pipeline, so TAGE matches branch histories of increasing length against tagged tables and uses the longest match.

main.title: Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution
main.why: CPUs run ahead on predicted branches and discard wrong work, but Spectre shows that work leaves cache traces that leak another program's secrets.

further.title: Mitigating Spectre and Other Security Threats: The Cloudflare Workers Security Model

main.title: Flipping Bits in Memory Without Accessing Them: An Experimental Study of DRAM Disturbance Errors
main.why: As DRAM cells shrink they disturb their neighbors, and this RowHammer study shows repeatedly opening one row flips bits in nearby rows on most modules.

further.title: Introducing Half-Double: New hammering technique for DRAM Rowhammer bug

main.why: Hardware counters traced Jira's slowdown on Graviton to L3 misses and TLB walks, so Atlassian shrank the JIT code cache and enabled huge pages.

further.title: Adopting Arm at Scale: Transitioning to a Multi-Architecture Environment

main.title: A Low-Overhead Coherence Solution for Multiprocessors with Private Cache Memories
main.why: Broadcasting every cache write saturated the shared bus, so the protocol later named MESI marks blocks exclusive or shared and invalidates only for shared ones.

further.title: Seeing through hardware counters: a journey to threefold performance increase

main.title: Shared Memory Consistency Models: A Tutorial
main.why: Write buffers, caches and compilers reorder memory accesses, so this tutorial explains the relaxed consistency models and the fences that restore order.

further.title: x86-TSO: A Rigorous and Usable Programmer's Model for x86 Multiprocessors

main.why: Container launches made every core fight over the kernel's mount lock, worst on dual-socket, hyperthreaded and mesh-interconnect CPUs, so Netflix cut the mounts per layer.

main.title: Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures
main.why: Peak compute says little when memory bandwidth limits a kernel, so the Roofline model bounds performance by the operations done per byte moved.

main.title: In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit
main.why: Neural network inference was outgrowing Google's datacenters, so the TPU drops caches and speculation for a large matrix unit and software-managed memory.

Inside the hardware and co-design of MTIA

main.title: Profiling a warehouse-scale computer
main.why: Benchmarks did not look like datacenter code, so Google profiled its live fleet and found instruction-fetch stalls and many cycles in shared low-level libraries.

main.title: Cores that don't count
main.why: Some cores in a large fleet silently compute wrong results that factory tests missed, so Google argues software must detect and isolate them.
